extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for designing and writing film stories and screenplays, covering story substance, structure, style, audience shaping, and specific scene-design rules (e.g., Inciting Incident placement and quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is about principles, not rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about principles. not rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish principles (timeless works) from rules (prescriptive 'must do' formulas). Learn the underlying tenets that shape the art so you can be well-made within those principles; master the form rather than blindly obeying recipes. Artists should use principles to liberate talent, not follow checklists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypes, not stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: The archetypal story unearths a universally human experience, then wraps itself inside a unique, culture-specific expression. A stereotypical story reverses this pattern: it confines itself to a narrow, culture-specific experience and dresses in stale, nonspecific generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for archetypal conflicts and human truths that travel across cultures while supplying fresh, specific detail. Anti-pattern: relying on familiar settings/characters/actions (clichés) that limit audience empathy. Examples: LIKE WATER FOR CHOCOLATE as archetypal; cautionary example of local custom-based stories that don't translate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and economy of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about thoroughness, not shortcuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screenwriting requires as much time and care as long-form writing; economy is key—express the maximum in the fewest possible words. Rewriting and ruthless cutting are essential. Pascal anecdote: brevity takes time. Anti-pattern: quick, sprawling first drafts that never get to a professional finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft is learnable; face realities, not mysteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about the realities, not the mysteries of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story craft is public and teachable (Aristotle onward). The screen exposes flaws (camera is an X-ray), so study and technique matter. There's no secret; skill comes from study, analysis, and practice, not mystique or innate 'inspiration' alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the art, not second-guess the marketplace
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about mastering the art, not second-guessing the marketplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot reliably predict what will sell. Focus on surpassing quality and original vision rather than formulaic trend-chasing. High quality work attracts representation and production; unfinished or rushed work invites tampering and poor outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and shape the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about respect, not disdain, for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the audience as intelligent and emotionally receptive: shape the story to express your vision while satisfying audience desires. Keep ahead of their sharp perceptions; anticipate their reactions and use the story to elicit full emotional and rational responses. Anti-pattern: talking down to the audience or misjudging their intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality = confluence of content and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality is the confluence of content and form - distinctive choices of subject plus a unique shaping of the telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop both fresh substance (setting, characters, ideas) and innovative form (selection and arrangement of events). Avoid eccentricity-for-its-own-sake; difference without purpose is hollow. Great writers fuse content and formal choices into a unique personal style (examples of auteurs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and practice the craft; avoid undereducation
rubrics_metrics.description: Too many would-be writers rush to the typewriter without first learning their craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study theory and practice (dramaturgy, story principles) through reading, apprenticeship, theatre, or formal study. Novices who rely solely on 'instinct' often produce work driven by unconsciously absorbed clichés. Anti-pattern: starting without studying structure, progression, values, and character design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design story around clear dramatic fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the total creative effort represented in a finished work, 75 percent or more of a writer's labor goes into designing story. Who are these characters? What do they want? Why do they want it? How do they go about getting it? What stops them? What are the consequences?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize defining protagonist(s), desires, motivations, antagonism, obstacles, progression, crises, and consequences. Story design tests maturity and insight and requires both vivid imagination and analytical thought. Anti-patterns: lack of progression, false motivation, redundant characters, holes in causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exposition-heavy openings; practice extreme economy
rubrics_metrics.description: How much does the audience need to know about the protagonist and his world to have a full response? Ingmar Bergman's extreme economy shows that less is often more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't over-explain or pack openings with extraneous backstory. Let the audience infer and fill in gaps. If you delay the Central Plot, use meaningful subplot material rather than long expository setup. Anti-pattern: long, tedious expository sequences that bore the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident: placement timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Where to place the Inciting Incident: as a rule of thumb, the first major event of the Central Plot occurs within the first 25 percent of the telling (standard for a two-hour feature: within the first half-hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the Central Plot's Inciting Incident as soon as possible—but not until the moment is ripe. If it arrives too soon the audience may be confused; too late and boredom results. Use subplots to engage if the main plot must be delayed. Examples: JAWS (starts immediately), TAXI DRIVER (later), ROCKY (half-hour setup).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident: required qualities and function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Inciting Incident must 'hook' the audience; it must upset the balance of forces in the protagonist's life, arouse in the protagonist the desire to restore balance, and raise the Major Dramatic Question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the Inciting Incident projects the Obligatory Scene (Crisis) into the audience's imagination. Ask: Does it radically upset the protagonist's life? Does it inspire conscious and/or unconscious desires that launch the quest? Is it germane to the world, characters, and genre? It can be minute (a look, a gesture) or massive (an explosion) depending on context. Examples: ORDINARY PEOPLE (French toast/garbage disposal), Kafka, KRAMER VS. KRAMER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subplots strategically to sustain audience engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Central Plot's Inciting Incident arrives much later than the opening, a subplot may be needed to engage audience interest while the main plot is prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce subplots that are compelling and relevant so waiting for the main plot doesn't cause boredom. Examples: TAXI DRIVER's assassination subplot, ROCKY's love subplot, CASABLANCA's multiple subplots in Act One.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadowing through projection of the Obligatory Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: With each line of dialogue or image of action you guide the audience to anticipate certain possibilities, so that when events arrive, they somehow satisfy the expectations you've created. The primary component of foreshadowing is the projection of the Obligatory Scene (Crisis) into the audience's imagination by the Inciting Incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant anticipatory elements early so payoffs feel earned. Use dialogue, images, and structural cues to shape expectation toward the Crisis/Obligatory Scene. Anti-pattern: surprises that feel unmotivated because they weren't properly foreshadowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control: avoid false motivation, holes, and clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of progression, false motivation, redundant characters, empty subtext, holes, and other such story problems are the root causes of a bland, boring text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate for logical progression, credible and strong motivations, meaningful subtext, and necessary characters. Fix holes and eliminate clichés. A strong story usually survives poor surface prose; but poor story design cannot be rescued by polished dialogue alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating the Inciting Incident: stretch toward extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating the Inciting Incident ask: What is the worst possible thing that could happen to my protagonist? How could that turn out to be the best possible thing? Or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'best/worst' permutations to discover dramatic reversals that fuel the protagonist's arc. Consider cycles of reversal (best -> worst -> possible salvation) to deepen stakes. Examples: KRAMER VS. KRAMER, AN UNMARRIED WOMAN, DEATH IN VENICE, THE GODFATHER PART II.
